title: London’s Millennium Bridge closed after two days because walkers synced up
body: The Millennium Bridge, a 325-metre steel suspension footbridge across the Thames, opened on 10 June 2000; about 90,000 people crossed that day, up to 2,000 at a time, and the deck swayed sideways by up to about 70 millimetres. Walkers unconsciously matched their steps to the sway, and each synchronised footstep pushed the bridge a little harder: a feedback loop known as **synchronous lateral excitation**, which the designers had not anticipated. The bridge closed on 12 June. Engineers fitted 37 fluid-viscous dampers and 52 tuned mass dampers for about £5 million, and the ‘Wobbly Bridge’ reopened on 22 February 2002 and has not swayed significantly since.

slides.question: How many dampers did engineers add to tame the sway?
slides.explanation: 37 fluid-viscous dampers and 52 tuned mass dampers, 89 in all, fitted between May 2001 and January 2002 for about £5 million.

slides.heading: The fix: 89 dampers
slides.note: Installed between May 2001 and January 2002 for about £5 million

slides.heading: The feedback loop
slides.text: People tend to match their footsteps to a sway, and a crowd walking in step pushes the deck sideways at just the right moment, so the sway grows. Crowds of up to 275 people were used to test the fix before the bridge reopened.

slides.heading: Not the first time
slides.text: Similar wobbles had struck the Auckland Harbour Bridge and the Birmingham NEC Link bridge, but the effect was not anticipated by the Millennium Bridge’s designers, Arup, Foster + Partners and the sculptor Anthony Caro.

slides.question: What drove the sway on the Millennium Bridge?
slides.explanation: Synchronous lateral excitation: people matched their footsteps to the sway, which pushed it further. Unlike Tacoma Narrows, wind was not the driver.
